paras: The Pocomoke City disturbance of 1881 was a confrontation between white youths and Black men in Pocomoke City, Worcester County, Maryland, beginning on Saturday evening, August 27, 1881. After a Black man was knocked down and the youths reportedly threatened to drive Black residents out, 50 or 60 Black men paraded the streets two nights later. Writs followed for 52 of the Black men, and the Snow Hill Democratic Messenger dismissed reports of a "riot" as exaggerated.

On Saturday evening some white boys got into an altercation with a group of Black men, and one of the Black men was knocked down. According to the Black residents, as the paper put it, the white boys threatened to "clear em out" at some future time.

On Monday night, August 29, 50 or 60 Black men assembled and paraded the streets, saying they were "ready for em," a reference to the young whites of Saturday's row. No violence followed, and the constable, who also served as bailiff, ordered the paraders home.

On Tuesday writs were issued for 52 Black men who had taken part, or were supposed to have taken part, in the parade. Eleven who could not pay a small fine for "disorderly conduct" were sent to the jail at Snow Hill, and the paper reported them released on the night of September 2. The white boy said to have begun the disturbance was also fined.

The only account found is a short item in the Snow Hill Democratic Messenger of September 3, headlined "That 'Riot.'" The paper put "riot" in quotation marks and called the affair "very insignificant," setting itself against "exaggerated reports" that it said had circulated throughout the country, none of which appear in the coverage. It used the slur "mokes" for the Black men, yet it placed the start of the trouble with a white boy and reported the threat only as the Black residents' claim.
It also suggested the Pocomoke magistrate and constable chose mass writs as the most "fees ible" plan, adding that Snow Hill authorities would have arrested only the ringleaders.

accounts.label: Snow Hill county paper
accounts.gist: A minor quarrel between white boys and Black men, inflated by rumor and 'exaggerated reports'; the Black men's Monday parade was peaceful, and the Pocomoke officials overreached with 52 writs.

accounts.label: Black residents' claim (as reported)
accounts.gist: The white boys threatened to 'clear em out' at some future time, and the Black men paraded to show they were 'ready for em'.

framing.detail: Headlined 'That "Riot."', the Democratic Messenger minimized the affair, used the slur 'mokes', but said a white boy began it and criticized the mass arrests of Black men as a fee-seeking plan.
